title: Database Operations: DDL and Constraints
what_is_it: DDL (Data Definition Language) changes the SHAPE of the database, not its data: CREATE TABLE defines a new table, ALTER TABLE changes an existing one (ADD COLUMN, ALTER COLUMN ... SET NOT NULL/DEFAULT), DROP TABLE removes one entirely. Constraints - PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK - are rules the table itself enforces on every write, either declared at CREATE TABLE time or added later with ADD CONSTRAINT.
why_it_matters: This is how a schema evolves once real data is already in it - you rarely get a table 100% right on the first CREATE TABLE, and ALTER TABLE (plus constraints) is how you tighten the rules and add new columns without losing what's already there.
example:
ALTER TABLE products
    ADD CONSTRAINT products_price_positive CHECK (price > 0);
output:
ALTER TABLE
(no rows returned - this changes the schema, not the data)
common_mistakes: Trying ALTER COLUMN ... SET NOT NULL on a column that ALREADY has a NULL value in some existing row - Postgres checks every current row first and rejects the whole ALTER if even one violates it. That's exactly why adding a nullable column WITH a DEFAULT first (so every row gets a real value immediately) is the standard way to safely tighten to NOT NULL afterward.
mini_exercise: Why would ALTER TABLE ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE (name) on products FAIL if two existing products already happened to share the same name?
postgres_note: Postgres DDL is transactional - CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, and DROP TABLE can all be rolled back like any other statement, which most other databases (MySQL notably) don't support for DDL.
